content: 1. Patients with fluoroquinolone resistance, cavitary disease on radiography, or smear-positive sputum are included in the dataset. 2. The dataset also includes individuals who have been previously treated with second-line drugs or those who have not. 3. Both children (ages 0–14 years) and adults (including adolescents aged 10–19 years, if data is available) are represented. 4. Persons living with HIV, regardless of antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, are included. 5. Pregnant women and individuals with extrapulmonary tuberculosis are part of the dataset. 6. Patients with comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, or mental disorders are also included. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a shorter, all-oral regimen lasting 9–12 months, which includes bedaquiline. 8. Comparisons are made between the shorter WHO-recommended regimen, older longer regimens without new drugs, and longer regimens with new tuberculosis (TB) drugs. 9. Treatment outcomes assessed include successful treatment completion, bacteriological cure, adherence to treatment, treatment failure or relapse, survival or death, adverse reactions to anti-TB medications, acquisition of drug resistance, and relapse-free cure. 10. The primary research question evaluates whether a bedaquiline-containing all-oral regimen lasting 9–12 months achieves the same or better outcomes compared to the WHO-recommended shorter regimen. 11. Secondary analyses compare outcomes between patients treated with shorter regimens and those treated with longer regimens, including those with or without new TB drugs. 12. The rationale for shorter regimens is to reduce the burden on patients and healthcare systems, minimize costs, and avoid the toxicities associated with injectable agents. 13. Shorter regimens are particularly beneficial for patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) who are less complex cases, such as those without additional resistance patterns or prior second-line drug exposure. 14. Data from South Africa provides a unique opportunity to compare outcomes across different regimens delivered in the same healthcare setting. 15. The analysis includes data from the Electronic Drug-Resistant TB Register (EDRWeb) in South Africa, which contains detailed information on treatment history, drug resistance testing, and treatment outcomes. 16. The study focuses on patients who initiated shorter regimens in 2017 and longer regimens in the first half of 2017, ensuring at least six months of post-treatment follow-up for relapse detection. 17. Relapse detection involves cross-matching patient records within EDRWeb and linking them to national death registries to capture post-treatment mortality. 18. The IPD in MDR-TB 2019 dataset includes records from over 13,000 patients across 40 countries and is used for secondary analyses. 19. The EndTB observational study includes 1,094 patients treated with bedaquilineand/or delamanid-containing regimens between 2015 and 2017, with comprehensive data on treatment outcomes and adverse events. 20. Comparisons between South African cohorts and international datasets account for differences in resource settings and patient characteristics. 21. Regimen classifications are based on treatment duration and drug composition, with specific criteria for inclusion in the analysis. 22. The intervention regimen is defined as a shorter, all-oral, bedaquiline-containing regimen lasting 9–12 months without injectable agents. 23. Comparator regimens include the WHO-recommended short regimen, longer regimens without new drugs, and longer regimens with new drugs. 24. The study aims to establish whether shorter regimens are as effective as longer or injectable-containing regimens while minimizing adverse outcomes and improving patient adherence.
